conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion:** The claim that giving children more vaccines causes more autism is not supported by the evidence in the supplied results.

The most directly relevant study measured children’s *total vaccine-antigen exposure* from immunization records—not merely whether they received one vaccine—and found no association between higher exposure during infancy and autism risk. This addresses the “too many, too soon” hypothesis more directly than studies of a single vaccine.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23545349/

A 2014 evidence-based meta-analysis likewise concluded that vaccination was not associated with autism/ASD, including analyses of vaccine components and multiple vaccines.  
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0264410X14006367

Recent large-scale evidence is consistent with this: a Danish nationwide cohort of more than 1.2 million children found no association between exposure to aluminum-adsorbed childhood vaccines and neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism. This does not measure the total number of all vaccines exactly, but it tests a common proposed mechanism for increased-schedule risk.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40658954/

The supplied results do include a claim based on a cross-country correlation between numbers of infant immunizations and autism rates. Such ecological comparisons cannot establish that vaccines caused autism in individual children: countries differ in diagnosis, reporting, healthcare access, genetics, and many other factors.  
https://indepnews.org/en/italian-study-confirms-more-childhood-vaccines-more-autism/

Overall, the causal claim is contradicted by better-designed individual-level studies and evidence syntheses.
